opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few distinct limits worth separating out.

The first is just the shape of the returns. When you look at how performance improves with more inference compute, whether through longer chains of reasoning, sampling many candidates and picking the best, or search, you typically see something like log-linear gains. Each doubling of compute buys you roughly a constant increment of improvement. That's real and useful, but it means costs grow exponentially for linear progress. At some point you're spending enormous amounts per query for fairly modest gains, and that limits how far it's economically sensible to push.

The second limit is that inference scaling seems to work best where you can verify answers. In math, coding, or problems with checkable solutions, generating lots of attempts and filtering them pays off, because you can tell which attempt is right. In domains where verification is hard, like open-ended research judgment, strategy, or anything where feedback comes slowly from the real world, extra thinking time helps much less. The model can deliberate longer, but if it has no reliable signal about whether it's on the right track, it may just elaborate confidently in the wrong direction.

Third, there's a ceiling set by the underlying model. Inference compute amplifies capabilities the model already has to some degree. It helps the model use its knowledge and skills more reliably and combine them more carefully. But it doesn't easily give the model knowledge or intuitions it fundamentally lacks. So there's a tight coupling between training compute and how much you can extract from inference compute. A weaker base model hits diminishing returns sooner. That's one reason I don't think inference scaling replaces training scaling. They're complements.

Fourth, there are practical constraints: latency, and the hardware you need to serve these workloads. If an answer takes hours of reasoning, that's fine for some tasks and useless for others. And serving long contexts at scale is memory- and bandwidth-intensive, so it competes for the same chips you'd otherwise use for training or for serving more users.

That said, I'd be careful not to overstate these limits. A lot of what looks like a ceiling today reflects how immature the techniques still are. Much of the progress has come from training models to reason better, so a given amount of thinking becomes more productive. If that continues, the effective returns to inference compute can keep improving even if the raw scaling curve looks logarithmic. There's also an important feedback loop: you can use expensive inference to generate high-quality reasoning traces and solutions, then train on them, which distills that capability back into the model. So inference compute isn't only something you spend at deployment. It can become a way to improve the next generation of models.

So my overall view is that inference scaling is a substantial and durable lever, especially for verifiable tasks, but it runs into steep cost curves, weak verification in many domains, and dependence on the strength of the base model. The most interesting dynamics come from how it interacts with training, not from treating it as a standalone path.

r001.rationale: It says a weaker base model hits diminishing returns sooner and explicitly says inference scaling does not replace training scaling; the two are complements.

r002.rationale: It says inference scaling works best when answers are verifiable and helps much less when there is no reliable signal for whether the model is on track.

r003.rationale: It gives no tentative Epoch estimate or roughly two-orders-of-magnitude limit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few. The first thing to say is that inference scaling clearly works to some degree. If you let a model think longer, sample more, search over candidate solutions, verify them, you get better performance on a lot of tasks. And that's been an important source of recent gains. But I think people sometimes talk about it as if it's this unbounded new axis, and I'm somewhat skeptical of that.

One limit is just the nature of the scaling relationship itself. When we've looked at this, what you typically see is something like log-linear improvements: each doubling of inference compute buys you a roughly constant increment in performance. So the returns diminish fairly quickly. Going from one sample to ten is great, going from a thousand to ten thousand is much less exciting, and at some point you're spending enormous amounts of compute for very marginal gains. And it's worth remembering that a model that's one or two orders of magnitude larger in training compute might achieve the same improvement at a fraction of the inference cost per query, so there's a real tradeoff frontier there rather than a free lunch.

A second limit is that inference scaling depends heavily on having some way to tell whether you've gotten the right answer. In math, in coding, in anything with a verifier or a clear reward signal, you can generate lots of candidates and select the good ones, or do search in a way that genuinely compounds. In domains where the feedback is fuzzy, where there's no cheap check, where you're producing an essay or a strategic judgment or a scientific hypothesis, it's much less clear that thinking longer gets you much. You can end up just sampling more confidently wrong outputs. So I'd expect the gains to be very uneven across tasks.

Third, there's a ceiling set by what the base model actually knows and can represent. Inference compute lets you more thoroughly exploit the capabilities that are already latent in the model, but it's not obviously creating new knowledge or new skills. If the model doesn't have the relevant concept, you can let it think for a week and it probably won't get there. So I tend to see inference scaling as a multiplier on training rather than a substitute for it.

And then there are more mundane economic constraints. Inference compute is a recurring cost; you pay it every time you use the system. Training compute is a one-off cost that gets amortized. So the economics push you toward putting compute into training when you expect a model to be used a lot, and only toward heavy inference when the task is high-value enough per instance. That caps how much of this you'll actually see deployed broadly.

So my overall view is: it's a real and meaningful lever, it helped a lot in the past couple of years, but I'd be surprised if it carried us very far on its own. I think the big picture is still dominated by the total compute going into training, the algorithmic progress, and the data, with inference scaling as a useful complement rather than the main story.

r001.rationale: The candidate says inference scaling has diminishing returns and treats it as a complement to training, not an indefinite substitute.

r002.rationale: It says gains are weaker in domains without a cheap, clear way to check answers, where additional inference may produce confidently wrong outputs.

r003.rationale: The candidate gives no estimate of roughly two orders of magnitude or attribution to Epoch.

astra-6.text:
I think the main limitation is that you need some way of turning additional computation into better answers. You can’t simply let a model run for longer and assume that it will make progress. It might repeat itself, explore unhelpful directions, or become more confident in a mistake.

One setting where this works quite naturally is when you can verify the answer. If you’re writing code and you have good tests, you can generate candidate solutions, test them, and use that feedback to improve. But for a question about strategy, or a scientific hypothesis that you can’t immediately test, it’s much harder to tell whether the extra reasoning has actually helped. The quality of that feedback becomes a constraint.

There are also diminishing returns. If the model has a reasonable chance of finding a solution, giving it more attempts can be useful. But if it’s missing a crucial concept, or all its attempts make the same underlying mistake, sampling more answers might not get you very far. You may need better training or new information.

And then there’s the economic limit: how much latency and cost are you willing to accept? You might happily pay for hours of computation to solve a valuable research problem, but you wouldn’t want that for every conversational response. So I’d expect inference scaling to be quite powerful in some domains, but its usefulness will depend on whether we can reliably turn that additional computation into progress.

r001.rationale: The response describes diminishing returns and says that when attempts share a missing concept or mistake, more sampling may not help and better training or information may be needed.

r002.rationale: It says inference scaling works naturally when answers can be verified, while unverifiable questions make it hard to tell whether extra reasoning helped and constrain feedback.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate of an upper bound in training-compute-equivalent terms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key limitation is that you need some way of turning additional computation into better answers. You can generate a thousand candidate solutions, but if you can’t reliably distinguish a good solution from a bad one, that doesn’t necessarily buy you very much.

In mathematics or programming, you often have a relatively cheap way to check an answer. You can run the code or verify a proof. That makes searching over many possible solutions quite powerful. For more open-ended tasks, evaluating the output can be almost as difficult as producing it. And if all your attempts share the same underlying mistake, sampling more of them won’t solve that problem.

There are also diminishing returns and practical constraints. Even if more computation improves performance, the improvement might become very small relative to the cost. And users may not want to wait minutes or hours for an answer.

So I’m optimistic that inference compute can deliver substantial gains, especially as models get better at using it. But it isn’t an automatic substitute for having the right capabilities in the first place. The question is how effectively a model can use extra time to search, check its work, and correct its mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response says inference compute is not an automatic substitute for the right capabilities and mentions diminishing returns, but it does not explicitly compare inference scaling with more training compute or say it cannot replace training indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It explains that when answers are hard to verify, generating more candidates may not improve results, linking unreliable answer checking to limited gains from added inference compute.

r003.rationale: The response gives no estimate of inference scaling in training-compute-equivalent terms and does not mention a roughly two-orders-of-magnitude ceiling.
